newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Sharp-suited TV pranksters pester Spain's elite.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sharp-suited TV pranksters pester Spain's elite.

text.p: A crack team of reporters dressed in black suits and wraparound sunglasses is striking terror into the hearts of Spain's elite with a weekly satirical television programme from which no one seems safe.
The show's cameras stalk politicians and celebrities at work and at public events.
High-profile victims of their pranks have included Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, U.S. film star Al Pacino and Cuban President Fidel Castro.
The satirists delighted in asking union leaders and Employment Minister Javier Arenas whether they had private pension plans, moments after they signed a deal securing the future of public pensions.

Fear of the dreaded all-male crew has prompted the government to bar them from parliament, whose corridors habitually throng with reporters ready to thrust tape recorders and microphones under the noses of ministers and deputies.
A large part of the gang's popular success is down to a sense of humour -- a quality noticeably absent from most Spanish media coverage.
"Caiga quien caiga" (loosely translated, "No holds barred") is the latest project of presenter Big Wyoming, a former doctor turned actor-writer-presenter with a devoted following in Spain.

The show is inspired by an Argentine programme of the same name and takes a light-weight approach to current affairs. But its chaotic mix of wacky camera angles, post-modern humour and film references has left more sedate viewers gasping for breath.
It has also succeeded in irking many of the country's top politicians, who have taken to excluding the reporters from their news conferences.
"We can hardly get in anywhere. People really fear us when they shouldn't," Wyoming told Reuters in an interview.
"Once they know us, and with the uniforms giving us away, just as we are about to go inside with our accreditations and everything, they say: 'You can't go through, your time is up.'"

The seven journalists model their razor-sharp outfits -- white shirt, black suit, tie and shades -- on those worn by the gangster characters in director Quentin Tarantino's cult film "Reservoir Dogs".

The obstacles they face include not only security guards but also obtrusive press officers who fear the "Tarantinos" -- as they have been dubbed by local media -- will hijack a minister's news conference and expose him to ridicule.

A government spokesman denied there was a concerted campaign to exclude "Caiga Quien Caiga" from press events. "I'm sorry to disappoint you, but I haven't even discussed this programme with my colleagues," he said.
But Wyoming said individual ministers had the power to decide who did and who didn't attend a briefing. The show's makers claim their bark is worse than their bite and deny accusations of malice.
"If we go to a press conference, people still think we are going to sabotage it, which is not true," said presenter Juan Jose de la Iglesia.
"We don't like people to end up looking ridiculous. We prefer it when a politician understands what you're asking him and gives you a clever answer, even if you end up looking stupid," he said.

"The problem is that the politicians here in Spain are excessively solemn and many of them have little mental speed, so if it's a slightly strange or impertinent question, there's no other way to do it."
Verbal stunts are not the only kind the reporters perform.

Typical challenges include trying to shake hands with untouchables like pop superstar Michael Jackson (they failed) or giving Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio a key-ring during a ceremony at which he was handed the keys of Madrid (he took it).

A "score" is treated to a slow-motion replay complete with crowd roar, while celebrities who agree to slip on the programme's trademark sunglasses receive the accolade "One of Us" flashed across the screen.
"We try to promote an intelligent sense of humour so that the victim of what we are doing can laugh as well," said de la Iglesia.
"In order for the programme to survive, we don't want there to be total confrontation with the politicians because in a way, we depend on them," agreed Wyoming.
The frontman admits that Spanish viewers have been slow to pick up the show's humour although he believes it could be very successful in the medium term.
The programme had an average rating of 18 percent in its first season but has only scraped 10 percent this autumn, partly because of strong competition from state television in its Sunday night slot.

Wyoming is aware the show's modern look and fast and furious visual gags may be a problem. "All these sorts of references are not references that everyone in Spain can manage or that everyone finds funny," he said.

"But in TV there is an imposition factor: you repeat the same formula again and again and people not only end up learning the same language but also start to enjoy it and finally they end up claiming it as their own."
